Where is the workbook, and what does it already know about this unit?

Part 1 · the plan

From a symptom to an open workbook

  1. Six stages and a reviewthe path every case follows, and what each stage hands on

  3. Workshop or Full, Thai or Englishsame project, two depths, three languages

Why this deck

A method beats a lucky guess

The OTS (operator training simulator) runs this unit. Its TE cases (Think EQUIPPED) hand you a symptom, not a cause.

TS Studio

TS = troubleshooting. The workbook walks one case through six stages.

Evidence

Trends, snapshot and event log pulled from the DCS.

Output

Report, team slides and a .woods.json project file.

DCS = distributed control system (the board screens). PVC = polyvinyl chloride resin, the powder this line conveys.

Woods & Marlin

Six stages, each with one deliverable

ReviewFundamentalshow it should behave
Stage 1Engagerun, park or stop
Stage 2Defineone testable statement
Stage 3Explorecauses as hypotheses
Stage 4Plantests that kill hypotheses
Stage 5Do itrun tests, fix, verify
Stage 6Look backsustain, cost, lessons

Part 2

What goes into each stage, and where does the simulator feed it?

Part 2 · the plan

Facts first, causes next, tests before any move

  1. Stages 0 and 1facts only, then how urgent: run, park or stop
  2. Stage 2 · Definewhat the symptom is and is not, one statement, a costed goal
  3. Review and Stage 3 · Explorethe governing equation, then every cause as a hypothesis
  4. Stage 4 · PlanS / D / N screening, then tests ranked by coverage and cost
  5. OTS data & evidencethree live pulls, or a CSV for offline copies

Stage 0 · The Problem

Write what was seen, with tag, number and time

Stage 0 asks what, who saw it, when and which tag.

Ground rule

No cause words yet. “Lumps block the line” belongs in Stage 3.

Interactive · sort each line

Fact or opinion?

A fact carries a tag, a number and a time; anything with a cause in it is an opinion until tested.

Stage 1 · Engage

How urgent, and do we keep running?

Time-critical

A trip, blockage or relief lift arrives before diagnosis unless you act.

Safe-park

A reduced, stable state that stops the problem growing.

Stop line

The reading at which you park or stop, written before you start.

Decision options: run and investigate, safe-park and investigate, or shut down.

Stage 2 · Define

IS / IS NOT narrows the search

For each dimension: what it is, what it could be but is not, and the distinction.

The last column names hypotheses the distinction already kills.

Interactive · tick the parts

A testable statement has five parts

Drop any part and the statement stops being testable: the number against normal is what a test can disprove.

Stage 2 · desired final state

SMARTS-$: a goal you can check off

S, M
specific and measurable: tag, value, duration
PT-102 ≈ 47, 15 min
A, R
achievable with existing kit; why it matters
trip margin back
T
time limit
within the shift
S
safe: what must not happen on the way
no trip, no PSV lift
$
cost ceiling for the whole job
< USD 3 000

Review · fundamentals

Two relations decide what a pressure can mean

$\Delta P_{line} = \Delta P_{air} + \Delta P_{acc} + \Delta P_{fric,s} + \Delta P_{lift} \qquad v/v_{salt} \ge 1.1$
$\Delta P_{line}$
PT-102 minus silo pressure
kPa
$\Delta P_{air},\,\Delta P_{acc}$
air friction; accelerating resin at pick-up
kPa
$\Delta P_{fric,s},\,\Delta P_{lift}$
resin friction; lifting resin up risers
kPa
$v,\ v_{salt}$
air velocity; velocity below which resin drops out
m/s

Line in two bores: DN150 (nominal 150 mm) then DN200. XI-106 computes $v/v_{salt}$ at the DN200 start.

Stage 3 · Explore

Every cause idea goes on one of six bones

Each idea becomes WH-n (working hypothesis): “if this, then we should observe…”, plus a falsifier.

Interactive · click a cell to cycle S, D, N

One D on a solid fact kills a hypothesis

Four quick checks put a D on four of seven causes before any plant test is run.

Stage 4 · Plan

Rank survivors by P × S × T

$\text{rank} = P \times S \times T$
$P$
probability the cause is true, team judgment
1–5
$S$
severity if it is true and left alone
1–5
$T$
testability: how cheaply a test settles it
1–5

Severity 5 goes to the first tier whatever the product.

Stage 4 · Plan

Five kinds of action, four kinds of test

  • (a) decide NOT to do
  • (b) quick action
  • (c) stop the rapid change
  • (d) others collect information
  • (e) plant experiment
A
read existing data
free
B
look: field check
cheap
C
buy: lab or vendor
days
D
change: plant experiment
risky

Interactive · pick the tests

Cover every survivor for the least cost

T-1 and T-2 together settle all four survivors for USD 90 and 45 minutes.

What Part 2 settled

Part 3

How was TE-1 solved, from the first trend to the lessons?

Part 3 · the plan

One worked case, loaded from the menu

  1. The situation and the first 20 minuteswhat the trainee is given, and what the trends show
  2. From numbers to a statementdeviation, balance, where the extra resistance sits
  3. Two tests, then the fixa field check, an air test, and the verified repair
  4. Look back and hand incost ledger, lessons, report, slides, .woods.json

Example 3.1 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 3.1TE-1 · Pressure spikes in the conveying line

“Since the dryer changed its sieve screens the pick-up pressure jumps by 10–20 kPa every few minutes and falls back; twice this week PAH-102 has come in. The air flow and the feed look normal. What is wrong?”

FT-101 kg/s0.983PI-101 kPa g61.8
XI-106 –1.24PI-104 kPa g22.5

Interactive · Example 3.1 · drag the cursor

EXAMPLE 3.160 minutes of TE-1 on the simulator

Spikes ride on a design base, go on with more air (25–35 min) and stop after the fix at 40 min.

Example 3.1 · Explore 3.2

EXAMPLE 3.1How big, and where along the line?

$\Delta = PT_{now} - PT_{design} \qquad \text{closure} = \dot m_{out}/\dot m_{in}$
$\Delta = 65.5 - 47.3 = 18.2$ kPa, or $+38.5\%$deviation of PT-102 from design
PI-104 rises only $\approx 3$ kPaextra resistance sits between pick-up and step
$18.0 / 18.0 = 100\%$no resin lost on the way
XI-106 = 1.24 between spikesabove 1.1: the air is not marginal

Example 3.1 · Define 2.11

EXAMPLE 3.1The statement the team tested

The pick-up pressure PT-102 jumps from 47.5 to as much as 65.5 kPa g, 8 times in 20 min, and falls back within about 30 s, against a steady 47.3 at design, since the dryer changed its sieve screens, while FT-101, WI-110 and the base pressures stay on design.

Goal (SMARTS-$): PT-102 steady near 47 kPa g, no spike for 15 min, within the shift, under USD 3 000.

Example 3.1 · Plan 4.3

EXAMPLE 3.1Facts on file kill three, weaken a fourth

HypothesisKilling factStatus
WH-3 · feeder surgesEv-5: WI-110 steady before every spikekilled
WH-4 · PT-102 faultyEv-3, Ev-4: PI-101, FT-101 move tookilled
WH-7 · silo filter blindingEv-9: filter ΔP PDI-201A steadykilled
WH-2 · air too lowEv-4: XI-106 1.24; still testedweak
WH-1, WH-5, WH-6no D yetto test

Example 3.1 · Do it 5.0

EXAMPLE 3.1Each test was predicted before it ran

TestPredictionObservedVerdict
T-1 field check, lab samplehiss at flaps? moisture > 0.3 %?no hiss; 0.2 %; lumps on the D-100 gridkills WH-5, WH-6
T-2 air 0.983 → 1.080 kg/s, 10 minsaltation: spikes stop6 spikes in 10 min, XI-106 1.35kills WH-2

Only WH-1 survives: lumps and skins from the dryer.

Interactive · Example 3.1 · set the threshold

EXAMPLE 3.1Count spikes before, during T-2 and after the fix

Look back 6.1KPI = rises of PT-102 above its base per shift

At any threshold the count after 45 min is zero: the fix removed the cause, not just the symptom.

Example 3.1 · Do it 5.1, 5.4

EXAMPLE 3.1State the cause as a mechanism

  1. New sieve screens pass agglomerates and wall skins.
  2. They fall through RV-101 and catch at a bend.
  3. Resin piles behind: a short plug; the PD blower pushes harder.
  4. Air breaks it in about 30 s; the next lump repeats it.

Fix at 40 min: re-fit the correct screen, clean the D-100 grid. Air and feed untouched.

PD = positive displacement: the blower delivers its air volume whatever the line resistance.

Example 3.1 · Look back 6.4–6.5

EXAMPLE 3.1Cost against the goal, and the one rule

Safe-park, lost feed, operator time150
Dryer stop, fitter, grid cleaning600
Lump catcher, spike counter (MOC)2 000
Total, USD (goal < 3 000)2 750

Value: about USD 12 000 of blockages avoided.

Rule for the next shift

Spikes on a steady base, steady feed and air: check the feed before the air.

MOC = management of change.

Class Activity · Problems

Can you solve it yourself?

Class Activity · the plan

Two problems on the TE-1 data

  1. Problem 4.1 · the price of more airpractises Parts 2 and 3: why more air is a test, not a fix
  2. Problem 4.2 · is the permanent fix worth it?practises Part 3: ledger, value and payback
  3. Then the critical-thinking quizten questions across the whole deck, voted live

Problem 4.1 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 4.1What would “more air for a week” cost?

During test T-2 of TE-1 the conveying air was raised from 0.983 to 1.080 kg/s for 10 minutes. The DCS recorded:

ReadingBeforeDuring T-2
Blower power (kW)6882
II-101 peak (A)147163
Spikes per 10 min46

The overload trip of the blower motor is 176 A. Take electricity at USD 0.12 per kWh (assumed). (a) What would running the higher air for 168 h cost in extra energy? (b) How much current margin is left at the T-2 peak? (c) Is more air a fix?

Problem 4.1 · solution

PROBLEM 4.1Dearer, closer to the trip, and no cure

$E = \Delta W \times t \qquad \text{margin} = (I_{trip} - I_{peak})/I_{trip}$

$\Delta W$ = extra blower power (kW); $t$ = hours run (h); $I$ = motor current (A).

(a) $(82-68)\times168 = 2\,352$ kWh $\to$ USD 282every week, for nothing
(b) $(176-163)/176 = 7.4\%$against 16.5 % at the 147 A peak before
(c) No: the spikes went onlumps do not answer to air

Problem 4.1 · try it

PROBLEM 4.1How long can you afford to hide the cause?

Problem 4.1$E = \Delta W \times t$, cost $= E \times$ price

A month of “more air” costs about USD 1 200, close to half the whole TE-1 ledger, and still leaves the lumps.

Problem 4.2 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 4.2Is the lump catcher worth USD 2 000?

From Example 3.1 Ledger: safe-park USD 150, dryer stop and grid cleaning USD 600, lump catcher plus DCS spike counter USD 2 000. Goal: under USD 3 000.

One full blockage of the line stops conveying for about 3 h (54 t of resin) and needs purging; take its cost as USD 6 000 (assumed). Without a barrier, the next wrong screen would cause about one blockage a week until it is found.

(a) Does the ledger meet the goal? (b) After how many avoided blockages does the USD 2 000 pay back? (c) What else does the barrier buy?

Problem 4.2 · solution

PROBLEM 4.2It pays back before the first blockage ends

$\text{payback} = C_{barrier} / C_{blockage}$

$C$ = cost (USD): of the barrier, and of one blockage.

(a) $150 + 600 + 2\,000 = 2\,750 < 3\,000$goal met
(b) $2\,000 / 6\,000 = 0.33$ blockageone avoided blockage repays it three times
(c) Early warning: the spike counter alarmsthe next screen error is seen in minutes

Problem 4.2 · try it

PROBLEM 4.2When does the barrier stop being worth it?

Problem 4.2$\text{payback} = C_{barrier} / C_{blockage}$

Even one screen error a year and a cheap blockage repay the barrier within the year.

Key Takeaways

1

Write facts with tag, number and time; keep causes for Stage 3.

2

State the symptom against normal so a test can disprove it.

3

Kill hypotheses with free facts before you change the plant.

4

Write each prediction and kill rule before the test runs.

5

Save the .woods.json every session; hand in report and slides.
